title: Nginx Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Nginx lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Serving a static file
entries.summary: Nginx is a web server. It can answer a request by sending a file, such as index.html, without running a custom application backend.

example.code:
Request: GET /index.html
Nginx reads: the configured index.html file
Response: HTML for the browser

notes: Serving files is different from executing browser JavaScript on the server.

entries.name: Read the configuration structure
entries.summary: Nginx configuration uses directives and blocks. Some directives are valid only in specific contexts.
notes: A directive in the wrong context can make configuration validation fail.

entries.name: Document roots
entries.summary: root chooses the base directory used to find a requested file. The request path is normally added to that base.
notes: Do not serve a directory containing passwords or private project files.

entries.name: Index documents
entries.summary: index names files to try when a request refers to a directory. index.html is a common first page.
notes: An index directive does not create the file.

entries.name: Locations match request paths
entries.summary: A location block chooses handling for matching request paths. Simple prefix locations are useful for organising a static site.
notes: root and alias combine paths differently; do not interchange them without checking.

entries.name: Check files with try_files
entries.summary: try_files checks candidate paths and uses a final fallback when none exists. Static generated pages often need directory index handling.
notes: Do not rewrite every missing asset to HTML; a script request needs a script, not the home page.

entries.name: Use a helpful error page
entries.summary: A custom error page explains a missing route while retaining a useful HTTP status.
notes: Do not return a success status for every missing URL.

entries.name: Content types matter
entries.summary: A MIME type tells the browser what kind of file it received. Standard Nginx MIME mappings cover common web assets.
notes: A wrong content type can stop scripts, styles or WebAssembly from loading.

entries.name: Cache deliberate file versions
entries.summary: Caching lets browsers reuse files. Long caching works best for files whose names change when their contents change.
notes: Do not cache a frequently updated HTML page for a year without a plan to refresh it.

entries.name: Read access and error logs
entries.summary: An access log records requests. An error log records problems such as missing permissions or invalid configuration.
notes: Avoid exposing logs publicly or recording unnecessary sensitive data.

entries.name: HTTPS protects the connection
entries.summary: HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt traffic between the browser and server. A certificate identifies the hostname for that connection.

example.code:
Browser -> encrypted HTTPS connection -> server
Certificate: must match the intended hostname
Keys: kept private on the server side

notes: Do not copy a real private key into a tutorial or public repository.

entries.name: Validate before reload
entries.summary: A configuration test can catch syntax problems before the server tries to use a new configuration. Reloading is a separate action.
notes: Do not restart or reload someone else's server while practising.
